analogy.p: Lossless compression is like vacuum-packing your clothes: everything you packed is still there and comes out exactly as it went in, but the case only shrinks by a certain amount. Lossy compression is like throwing out half of your clothes to make the case much lighter: you save a lot more room, but the clothes you left behind are gone for good. RLE is like writing '5 identical socks' on a list instead of listing each sock. The analogy breaks down because lossy compression chooses what to remove using rules about what people are unlikely to notice, whereas a packer chooses by guesswork, and decompression cannot get the discarded items back.

bullets: Know the **purpose of compression**: smaller files, so less storage and faster transfer.
Know the **two types**: lossy and lossless, and what each does to the original data.
Know **examples of each**: lossless (PNG, ZIP, FLAC, GIF) and lossy (JPEG, MP3, MP4).
Be able to **compress and decompress** a short string or row of pixels using run length encoding.
Be able to **choose and justify** which type to use for a given file or purpose.
Know the **advantages and disadvantages** of each type, including the effect on quality and file size.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.2 requires you to understand **why files are compressed** and to be able to describe and compare **lossy** and **lossless** compression. You should know what each type does to the data, that lossless allows the original to be rebuilt exactly while lossy permanently removes data, and be able to choose the more suitable type for a situation and justify it. Run length encoding (RLE) is the standard lossless example that you may be asked to apply by hand. This is examined as 1 to 2 mark definitions, 4 mark compare questions, and 6 mark discussion questions linking compression to storage, transmission and quality.

bullets: **Less storage space** is needed, so more files fit on a device or server.
Files **upload and download faster** because fewer bits are sent.
Less **bandwidth** is used, which is cheaper and means more users can share a connection.
**Streaming** audio and video is smoother because the data arrives fast enough to play without buffering.
**Email attachments** and websites with many images are easier to send and load.
Compression can reduce the cost of **cloud storage and data transfer** for companies.
core.p: **Compression** means reducing the size of a file so that it uses fewer bits. This matters because storage space and network bandwidth are both limited and cost money. A smaller file takes up less room on a device, so more files can be stored. It also takes less time to send across a network, which makes web pages load faster, lets video and music **stream** without buffering, and reduces the amount of **bandwidth** used. Compression is applied to almost every file you meet: photos, songs, films, web pages and downloads are nearly all stored in compressed formats.

bullets: **Lossless**: no data is lost; the original can be **perfectly restored** (reconstructed bit for bit).
**Lossy**: some data is **permanently removed**; the original **cannot** be restored.
Lossless gives a **moderate** reduction in size; lossy usually gives a **much bigger** reduction.
Lossless keeps **full quality**; lossy reduces quality (more compression means lower quality).
**Decompression** is the process of turning a compressed file back into a usable form.
Both types need a **program or codec** to compress and to decompress.
core.h: The two types: lossy and lossless
core.p: Compression is done by an **algorithm**, a set of rules that works out how to represent the data in fewer bits. The big difference between the two types is whether any information is **thrown away** along the way. **Lossless** compression reduces the file size without losing any data, so when the file is **decompressed** the original is rebuilt exactly. **Lossy** compression gets a smaller file by **permanently removing** some data that is judged less important, so the decompressed file is only an approximation of the original and the removed data can never be recovered.

bullets: Nothing is lost, so the file can be **restored exactly** to the original.
Used where **accuracy is vital**: text documents, spreadsheets, program code, databases, legal and medical records.
Formats: **PNG, GIF** (images), **FLAC** (audio), **ZIP** (any file).
Methods include **run length encoding** and **dictionary or Huffman coding**, which find repeated patterns.
**Disadvantage:** the file is **larger** than the same file compressed with lossy compression.
**Advantage:** can be compressed and decompressed **repeatedly** without any loss of quality.
core.p: Lossless compression looks for **patterns and repetition** in the data and stores them in a shorter way, without discarding anything. Because nothing is removed, the file can always be restored exactly, which is essential when every bit matters. Examples of formats are **PNG and GIF** (images), **FLAC** (audio) and **ZIP** (general files). The amount of saving depends on how much repetition there is, so lossless compression cannot shrink every file by much, and a file with very little repetition might hardly shrink at all.

bullets: A **run** is a block of identical consecutive values; RLE stores the **count and the value**.
Example: AAAABBBCCDAA becomes **4A3B2C1D2A**.
To **decompress**, write each value out the number of times given: 3W5B1W becomes WWWBBBBBW.
Works best with **long runs**: simple graphics, logos, icons and black-and-white images.
Works poorly on **detailed data** with little repetition, such as photos or random text; the output can be **bigger** than the input.
RLE is **lossless** because the exact original can always be rebuilt from the pairs.
core.p: **Run length encoding** is the standard example of lossless compression. A **run** is a sequence of the same value repeated one after another. Instead of storing the value every time, RLE stores **how many times it repeats followed by the value**. For example the string AAAABBBCCDAA (12 characters) is stored as 4A3B2C1D2A (10 characters). To decompress, you simply expand each pair back out, so no information is lost. RLE works best on data with **long runs**, such as an image with large areas of the same colour. It works badly on data with few repeats: the string ABCD becomes 1A1B1C1D, which is **bigger** than the original.

bullets: **Dictionary coding**: repeated patterns are stored once and replaced by short references.
**Huffman coding**: frequently used values get **shorter** codes; rare values get **longer** codes.
Both are **lossless** because the table lets the original be reconstructed exactly.
The **table or dictionary must be stored** with the file so the data can be decompressed.
Text compresses well because letters such as 'e' and 'th' repeat often.
Different compression algorithms suit **different kinds of data**.
core.h: Other lossless methods: dictionary and Huffman coding
core.p: RLE is not the only way to compress losslessly. **Dictionary methods** build a table of patterns that appear repeatedly in the file and replace each occurrence with a short reference to the table entry. **Huffman coding** gives the **most common** characters or values the **shortest** binary codes and rarer ones longer codes, so the average number of bits used per item falls. In both cases the code table is stored with the file, which lets the decompressor rebuild the original exactly. ZIP files use lossless techniques of this kind. You do not need to carry out these methods by hand, but you should know that they exist and that they are lossless.

bullets: Data is **permanently removed**, so the original **cannot be restored**.
Gives a **much smaller file** than lossless compression, ideal for **streaming and web use**.
**Quality is reduced**, and the more it is compressed the worse the quality gets.
Formats: **JPEG** (images), **MP3** (audio), **MP4** (video).
Only suitable where **small quality loss is acceptable**: not for text, code or data where every detail matters.
Repeatedly editing and **re-saving** a lossy file causes **further quality loss**.
core.p: Lossy compression achieves a much smaller file by **removing data that humans are unlikely to notice is missing**. The data that is removed is thrown away for good, so the original can **never** be recovered, and repeatedly compressing and re-saving a lossy file makes the quality worse each time. The degree of compression is usually adjustable: stronger compression gives a smaller file but lower quality. Lossy compression is ideal for **photos, music and video** that are being viewed or listened to, where a small loss in quality is acceptable in return for a big reduction in size.

bullets: Lossy image compression **removes fine detail** and similar colours that the eye is least likely to notice.
Can **reduce the colour depth**, so fewer bits are needed per pixel.
Can **reduce the resolution**, so there are fewer pixels to store.
**JPEG** is the common lossy format and is ideal for **photographs** on websites.
Too much compression causes **blockiness, blurring and banding**.
The original image **cannot** be recovered from a JPEG, so keep an uncompressed copy if you may edit it later.
core.p: For an image, lossy methods remove detail that the human eye is less likely to notice. This can mean **reducing the colour depth** (using fewer bits per pixel, so fewer colours), **reducing the resolution** (fewer pixels), or combining areas of similar colour into one, which removes **fine detail**. JPEG is the common lossy image format. The effect of too much compression is visible as a blocky or blurred picture with **banding** where smooth colour changes become steps. Because the file has fewer bits it is smaller, loads faster on a web page and uses less storage.

bullets: Removes sounds **humans cannot hear** (frequencies outside the range of hearing) and sounds **masked** by louder ones.
Can **reduce the sample rate** or **bit depth** to cut the number of bits per second.
**MP3** is the common lossy audio format; a typical MP3 is about **10%** of the size of an uncompressed CD recording.
Smaller files let a **phone store thousands of songs** and let music **stream without buffering**.
At very high compression the sound becomes **tinny or distorted**.
**FLAC** is a **lossless** alternative used by people who want exact quality, but its files are larger.
core.p: For sound, lossy methods take advantage of the limits of **human hearing**. They remove frequencies that are **too high or too low to hear**, and quiet sounds that are **masked** by louder ones at the same time. They can also **reduce the sample rate and bit depth**, so fewer bits are needed for each second of sound. MP3 is the best-known lossy audio format. A typical MP3 is roughly one tenth the size of an uncompressed CD-quality recording, which is why thousands of songs can fit on a phone and why music streams quickly. The cost is that some of the original detail is gone for good.

bullets: **Data:** lossless loses **none**; lossy **permanently removes** some.
**File size:** lossless is **larger**; lossy is **much smaller**.
**Restoring the original:** possible with lossless; **impossible** with lossy.
**Quality:** lossless keeps **full quality**; lossy gives **reduced quality**.
**Typical uses:** lossless for **text, code, documents, medical images**; lossy for **photos, music, video streaming**.
**Examples:** lossless PNG, FLAC, ZIP; lossy JPEG, MP3, MP4.
core.p: Examination questions often ask you to **compare** the two types, so you need clear contrasting statements, each backed by a reason. The central trade-off is between **file size and quality**. Lossy gives smaller files but sacrifices data for good; lossless keeps everything but saves less space. A good comparison uses linking words such as 'whereas' and 'however' and covers the effect on size, the effect on quality and whether the original can be restored.

bullets: **Program code or a word-processed document:** lossless, because losing data would **corrupt** it.
**Photos on a website:** lossy (JPEG), because small files **load quickly** and the loss is hardly noticeable.
**Music for a portable player:** lossy (MP3), because it gives a **small file** so many songs fit.
**A professional photographer's originals for editing:** lossless, because quality must be **kept**.
**Streaming video:** lossy, because it must use **limited bandwidth**.
**A logo with large flat areas of colour:** lossless (PNG/GIF) works well because there are **long runs**.
core.h: Choosing the right type of compression
core.p: To choose the right type, ask two questions: **does every bit of the original need to be kept?** and **how important is a small file size?** If a single missing bit would make the file useless (a program, a document, a spreadsheet, a legal record, a medical scan, a file you intend to edit again), you need **lossless**. If the file is only going to be viewed or heard, and size matters more than perfect quality (a web photo, a streamed film, a song on a phone), **lossy** is the better choice. In an exam, give the type, then the reason that is specific to the scenario.

bullets: **Percentage reduction** = (original size − compressed size) ÷ original size × 100.
Example: 8 MB compressed to 2 MB saves 6 MB, which is 6 ÷ 8 × 100 = **75%**.
**Compression ratio** = original : compressed, so 8 MB to 2 MB is **4 : 1**.
**Transfer time = size in bits ÷ speed in bits per second**: a 15 MB file (120 megabits) on a 10 Mbps connection takes **12 s**; compressed to 1.5 MB it takes **1.2 s**.
Use the **same units** for original and compressed sizes before calculating.
Compression **saves storage and transfer time** but has a small **cost in processing** to compress and decompress.
core.p: The saving from compression can be worked out as a **percentage reduction**, found by dividing the amount saved by the original size and multiplying by 100. It can also be given as a **compression ratio**, original size : compressed size. Smaller files also affect **transfer time**: time taken is file size in bits divided by the connection speed in bits per second, so a file one tenth of the size takes one tenth of the time. These calculations connect compression to the data unit work earlier in the specification.

bullets: **File size calculations:** compression reduces the result of width × height × colour depth or rate × depth × duration.
**Storage devices:** smaller files mean **more files on the same device** or a cheaper device.
**Networks and the internet:** compressed files **download and stream faster** and use less bandwidth.
**Image representation:** lowering **colour depth** or **resolution** is a simple form of lossy compression.
**Sound representation:** lowering **sample rate** or **bit depth** is a simple form of lossy compression.
**Ethics/practical:** lossy compression of images means the original quality is **lost for good**, so keep backups.
core.p: Compression connects directly to the earlier calculations of file size, because it is the main way of reducing the size those formulas produce. It also links to **secondary storage** (smaller files mean a smaller or cheaper device is enough), to **networks** (less bandwidth used, faster downloads), and to **data representation** (reducing colour depth, resolution, sample rate or bit depth is what some lossy methods do). A strong 6-mark answer ties the choice of compression to **both storage and network** consequences.

exam: **Define (2 marks):** lossy = some data is permanently removed (1) so the original cannot be restored (1); lossless = no data is lost (1) so the original can be rebuilt exactly (1).
**State/give (1 mark):** name an example format: lossy JPEG, MP3, MP4; lossless PNG, GIF, FLAC, ZIP.
**Why compress (2 marks):** smaller file needs less storage space (1); and takes less time/bandwidth to transmit or download (1).
**Apply RLE (2 to 3 marks):** write each run as count then value, include runs of 1, and check by decompressing your answer back to the original.
**Decompress (2 marks):** expand each pair, then count the total characters to check against the length given.
**Compare (4 marks):** use 'whereas' or 'however' and cover size, quality and whether the original can be restored (two matched points earns 4).

**Choose and justify (2 to 4 marks):** name the type, then give a reason **about the scenario** (for example 'lossy because a smaller file loads faster on the website and the small loss in quality is not noticeable').
**6-mark discuss:** give advantages and disadvantages of both types, link to storage, bandwidth, quality and the scenario, then give a reasoned conclusion.
**Calculations:** percentage reduction = saving ÷ original × 100; keep units the same; show working.
**Never write** only 'it makes the file smaller' for lossless: explain that it keeps all the data and can be restored.
**Model phrases:** 'permanently removes data', 'cannot be restored to its original', 'repeated patterns', 'reduces bandwidth', 'acceptable loss of quality'.

mistakes.r: State that some data is permanently removed and cannot be restored, which reduces quality.
mistakes.w: Saying lossy compression 'loses quality' without saying data is removed permanently.

mistakes.r: Lossless does reduce size by finding repeated patterns, but less than lossy, and no data is lost.
mistakes.w: Saying lossless compression does not make files smaller.

mistakes.r: It depends on the scenario: lossy for small files where some quality loss is acceptable, lossless where all data must be kept.
mistakes.w: Writing that lossy is 'better' or lossless is 'better' in general.

mistakes.r: Use the format given in the question; commonly count then value, e.g. 4A. Be consistent and clear.
mistakes.w: Writing RLE as just the letters with the count after, mixing up the order (A4).

mistakes.r: Every run is written with its count, including runs of 1: 4A3B2C1D2A.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to count single items in RLE (writing 4A3B2CD2A).

mistakes.r: Only lossless files can be restored exactly; lossy files cannot.
mistakes.w: Claiming compressed files can always be restored to the original.

mistakes.r: Say that a smaller file needs less storage and less bandwidth, so it downloads or streams faster.
mistakes.w: Giving 'it is quicker' as the whole answer for why compress.

mistakes.r: JPEG and MP3 are lossy; PNG, GIF, FLAC and ZIP are lossless.
mistakes.w: Saying a JPEG or MP3 is lossless.

mistakes.r: With little repetition RLE can make the data bigger (ABCD becomes 1A1B1C1D).
mistakes.w: Thinking RLE always shrinks the data.

summary: OCR J277 1.2 asks you to explain why files are compressed and to describe and compare lossy and lossless compression, including applying run length encoding and choosing the right type for a situation. It matters because compression decides how much storage and bandwidth a file needs, and it is examined as definitions, comparisons and 6-mark discussion questions.

terms.d: Reducing the size of a file so that it uses fewer bits of storage and takes less time to transmit.
Converting a compressed file back into a form that can be used.
Compression that reduces the file size without losing any data, so the original can be restored exactly.
Compression that permanently removes some data to make the file smaller, so the original cannot be restored.
A lossless method that replaces a run of identical values with a count and the value, e.g. AAAA stored as 4A.
A sequence of identical consecutive values in a set of data.
A lossless method that replaces repeated patterns with short references to entries in a stored table.
A lossless method that gives shorter binary codes to values that occur more often.
A set of rules or step-by-step instructions used to perform compression or decompression.
The amount of data that can be transmitted across a network connection in a given time.
Sending audio or video continuously over a network so it can be played while it is still being received.
Temporary storing of incoming data before it is played; delays happen when data arrives too slowly.
A common lossy image file format used for photographs.
A common lossy audio file format.
The original file size compared with the compressed size, e.g. 4 : 1.
The number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel.

worked.q: Compress the following row of pixels using run length encoding: WWWWWWBBBWWWW. State how many characters are saved. [3 marks]
steps: Split into runs: WWWWWW (6 W), BBB (3 B), WWWW (4 W).
Write each run as count then value: 6W 3B 4W.
Original has 13 characters, so the saving is 13 − 6 = 7 characters.

worked.ans: 75% reduction; the compressed file downloads in 4 seconds.
worked.q: A file is 8 MB. After compression it is 2 MB. Calculate the percentage reduction in file size, and say how long the compressed file takes to download on a 4 Mbps connection (1 byte = 8 bits). [4 marks]
steps: Compressed size in bits: 2 MB × 8 = 16 megabits.
Time = 16 ÷ 4 = 4 seconds (the original would take 64 ÷ 4 = 16 seconds).

worked.ans: Lossy for the website (small files, fast loading, acceptable quality loss); lossless for editing copies (no data lost, original quality kept).
worked.q: A photographer wants to put photos on a website and also keep copies for editing. Explain which type of compression she should use for each purpose. [4 marks]
steps: Because it makes the files much smaller (1), so pages load faster and use less bandwidth, and the small loss of quality is not noticeable on screen (1).
Editing copies: use lossless compression (e.g. PNG) or no compression (1), because no data is lost and the full quality is kept for editing.
